hero.tagline: One design system, five operations applications, light and dark themes — so operators learn the interface once.

metadata.team: Product, architecture and engineering stakeholders across Australia, Finland, USA and France

sections.plainTerms: Telecom companies run their networks using several separate software tools — one to plan changes, one to schedule them, one to launch step-by-step procedures, one to watch them run, and so on. Over time each tool had grown its own colours, buttons and layouts, so people moving between them kept having to relearn the screens. I built a shared 'kit of parts' — a design system — and moved all five tools onto it. Now they look and behave the same, and one setting switches every tool between light and dark mode.
sections.problem:
The network automation platform is a multi-application product covering assurance, performance and security. Its operations applications — including workflow management, scheduling, and MOP (Method of Procedure) launch and monitoring — had been built by different teams at different times, and each had drifted into its own visual style and interaction patterns.

For operators who move between these tools during a single network change, that inconsistency meant extra learning, extra hesitation, and more room for mistakes. For engineering, every new screen was designed and coded from scratch.

methods: Heuristic review of each application against a common set of usability principles
UI inventory: collecting every button, table, form and colour in use across the five apps
Working sessions with product, architecture and engineering stakeholders in four countries
Review of accessibility needs against WCAG guidelines
insights: The same task (filter, select, act) was presented differently in each app
Most visual differences came from hard-coded values that a shared token set could replace
Operators in control rooms need a dark theme; office users often prefer light — both had to be first-class
A shared component library would let teams ship new screens without redesigning basics

solution.approach:
I defined the design system in three layers. Design tokens hold the base decisions — colours, type sizes, spacing — as named values. Reusable components (tables, forms, dialogs, status chips) are built only from those tokens. UI standards document how components combine into common page patterns.

Because every colour comes from a token, light and dark themes are two token sets rather than two designs. Each application was then moved onto the shared system, with stakeholders reviewing each step from sketch to prototype to shipped UI.
keyFeatures: Design tokens for colour, typography and spacing, with light and dark sets
Reusable Angular component library built on the tokens
Documented UI standards and page patterns for all five applications
Accessibility built into components rather than added per screen
Mentoring for designers and developers adopting the system

design.system: Token-based design system shared across five operations applications, with light and dark themes.

learnings: Tokens first: once colours and spacing are named values, theming and consistency follow almost for free
Standardisation is a people project as much as a design one — regular reviews with every team kept adoption moving
Building accessibility into shared components fixes it once for every screen

hero.tagline: Cockpit screens that show field and change teams only what needs action — delivered through to customer sign-off.

metadata.team: Product, engineering and QA teams with global stakeholders

sections.plainTerms: When a telecom network is being changed, engineers on site and coordinators in the office need to know what is planned, what is running, and what is stuck. I designed 'cockpit' screens — like a car dashboard, they show only the things that need attention right now instead of long lists of everything. The app was taken all the way through UAT (User Acceptance Testing), the final stage where the customer's own users try it and formally sign it off.
sections.problem: Change coordination and field-operations work involves many parallel activities, each with its own status. Showing all of them at once buries the few items that actually need someone to act — and people working on site have little time and small screens.

methods: Workflow mapping of change coordination and field-operations tasks with product owners
Review of existing screens to separate 'needs action' from 'for information'
insights: Users' first question is 'what needs me now?' — not 'what is the full list?'
Status must be readable at a glance, on both desktop and mobile
Coordinators and field engineers need different views of the same data

solution.approach: I designed dashboards and cockpit screens around actionable items: anything that needs a decision or a response rises to the top, while routine progress stays one step away. Layouts are responsive so the same information works on a laptop in the office and a phone in the field. I then led the front-end delivery through testing to UAT closure.
keyFeatures: Cockpit view that surfaces only items needing action
Dashboards for change coordination
Responsive layouts for field use on mobile
Clear, consistent status indicators built on the shared design system

design.process: Workflow mapping → cockpit concept → prototypes → stakeholder review → front-end build → UAT.

learnings: Designing for 'what needs action' cuts noise more than any visual polish
Field users set the bar: if it works on a phone mid-task, it works everywhere
Owning delivery through UAT keeps design intent intact in the shipped product

hero.tagline: AI and automation do the routine work; people always see what happened and can step in.

metadata.team: Product, architecture and engineering stakeholders across four countries

sections.plainTerms: This platform connects different network tools so work can flow between them automatically. 'Low-code' means users build or change those flows by arranging ready-made blocks on screen rather than writing program code. Some steps are suggested or done by AI and automation, so every action shows one of three states — done automatically, waiting for a person to review, or approved — and a person can override it at any point. That is 'human-in-the-loop': the machine helps, but a human stays in charge.
sections.problem: As more operations work becomes automated and AI-assisted, operators need to trust what the system is doing. If it is unclear whether an action ran automatically or was approved by someone, people either stop trusting the automation or stop checking it — both are risky on a live network.

methods: Use-case workshops with product and architecture stakeholders
Mapping each automated step to who is accountable for it
Prototype reviews of action states and override flows
insights: Operators need to see who or what took an action, and when
Every automated step needs a visible way for a person to stop or change it
Non-developers should be able to adjust flows without code

solution.approach: Phase I delivered the integration platform's core screens. For AI-assisted operations I defined a small, consistent set of interaction patterns: three clear states — automated, in review, approved — shown the same way everywhere, with a human override always available. Phase II, which I now lead, turns the platform into a modular low-code application where flows are assembled from building blocks.
keyFeatures: Consistent states for automated, in-review and approved actions
Human override available at every step
Modular, block-based low-code flow building (Phase II)
Built on the shared design system

design.process: Phase I live; Phase II low-code application in progress.

learnings: Trust in automation comes from visibility: show what happened and let people undo it
A few action states used consistently beat many states used loosely
Low-code only works if the building blocks match how operators already think about their tasks

hero.tagline: Bringing a production portal up to a current, supported framework and closing its security gaps.

metadata.team: Engineering team with product and security stakeholders

sections.plainTerms: Angular is the toolkit the portal's screens are built with. Like the software on your phone, it needs regular updates — older versions stop receiving security fixes. I led the move to a current version and fixed the security weaknesses ('vulnerabilities') found in the portal's own code and in the third-party building blocks ('libraries') it depends on.
sections.problem: The operations portal was running on an older Angular version. Staying on it meant fewer security updates and a growing list of known vulnerabilities in the portal's dependencies.

methods: Dependency and vulnerability audit of the front-end
Review of breaking changes between Angular versions
Planning the upgrade path with engineering and product
insights: Most vulnerabilities came from outdated third-party libraries, not the portal's own code
Upgrading the framework and fixing vulnerabilities together avoided doing the work twice

solution.approach: I planned and led the upgrade step by step through Angular versions, updating or replacing vulnerable dependencies along the way and fixing code affected by framework changes.
keyFeatures: Angular framework upgrade
Vulnerable dependencies updated or replaced
Code updated for framework changes

learnings: Regular, smaller upgrades are far cheaper than rare, large ones
Pairing a framework upgrade with a security audit gives one clear, defensible plan

hero.tagline: Bringing AI coding assistants into a design and front-end team — with mentoring, not just licences.

sections.plainTerms: These are AI tools that help write software. GitHub Copilot and Cursor suggest code while a developer types, a bit like autocomplete for programming. v0 and Bolt can turn a written description or a rough sketch into a first working screen. I introduced them to the team and coached designers and developers on using them well — with a person still reviewing what ships.
sections.problem: AI coding assistants were becoming widely available, but without guidance people either avoided them or used them without the review habits that keep quality high.

methods: Hands-on trials of each tool on real UI tasks
Pairing sessions with designers and developers
insights: Different tools suit different jobs: in-editor help vs. generating a first screen
Designers benefit as much as developers, especially for quick prototypes

solution.approach: I introduced GitHub Copilot, Cursor, v0 and Bolt to the team and mentored people on where each one fits, how to prompt it, and how to review its output before it ships.
keyFeatures: GitHub Copilot and Cursor for in-editor coding help
v0 and Bolt for generating first-draft UI
Mentoring on prompting and reviewing AI-generated code

learnings: AI output is a first draft — review habits matter more than the tool

hero.tagline: From concept to delivery for 2,500+ users — and in-house tools that won three company awards.

sections.plainTerms: An intranet is a company's private website for its own staff. I designed and built it, along with everyday in-house tools — for logging work hours, running performance reviews and running surveys. The time tracking tool cut the effort of recording hours and charging them to the right budget ('cost recharge') by 90%. I also designed a 'GUI-based' automation tool, which lets people automate repetitive tasks by clicking through screens instead of writing scripts.
sections.problem: Staff across Nokia's global delivery centres relied on a mix of disconnected internal tools and manual processes for everyday work like booking effort, recharging costs and performance reviews.

methods: Usability reviews of existing internal tools
Rollout planning for the India global delivery centre
insights: Manual effort booking and cost recharge consumed significant time every cycle
A single portal entry point made niche tools easier to find and use

solution.approach: As usability specialist and UI designer-developer, I took the intranet portal and a pack of niche applications from concept to creation, planned the India GDC rollout, and extended delivery to other global centres. Alongside it I designed the time tracking, performance management and survey applications, a GUI-based automation tool, a tools gallery and a monthly flipbook newsletter.
keyFeatures: Intranet portal and niche applications for 2,500+ users
Time Tracking Tool for effort booking and cost recharge
Performance management and survey applications
GUI-based automation tool
Tools gallery and monthly flipbook newsletter

learnings: Internal tools deserve the same usability care as customer products — the time savings compound
Planning the rollout is part of the design: adoption across centres depended on it
